name: Time & space complexity (Big O, Omega, Theta)
overview: Asymptotic notation describes how a program's runtime or memory usage grows as the input size increases. Big O gives an upper bound, Omega gives a lower bound, and Theta gives a tight bound when both match. These tools let you reason about performance without depending on a specific machine.
why: Every interviewer expects you to state time and space complexity for your solution, and comparing algorithms by their Big O is the core of choosing between approaches. Failing to analyze complexity signals weak fundamentals.
when: Reach for asymptotic analysis whenever you propose a solution or need to decide between multiple approaches. Use it to reject brute-force solutions and justify optimizations before writing any code.

concepts.name: Big O (worst case)
concepts.description: Upper bound on growth; O(n) means the work scales at most linearly with input size.

concepts.name: Big Omega (best case)
concepts.description: Lower bound on growth; Omega(n) means the work scales at least linearly.

concepts.name: Big Theta (tight bound)
concepts.description: When upper and lower bounds match, giving a precise growth rate such as Theta(n log n).

concepts.name: Dominant term
concepts.description: Keep only the fastest-growing term and drop constant factors when simplifying, e.g. 3n^2 + 5n becomes O(n^2).

concepts.name: Logarithmic growth
concepts.description: Halving the search space each step, as in binary search, produces O(log n) work.

patterns.name: Loop counting
patterns.description: Count how many times each nested loop runs in terms of input size.

patterns.name: Nested loops
patterns.description: Two independent loops over n inputs usually multiply to O(n^2).

patterns.name: Halving loops
patterns.description: A loop that divides the work each step is logarithmic.

examples.title: Counting loop iterations
examples.problem: Estimate the growth rate of a loop that runs from 1 to n in steps doubling each time.
examples.explanation: The loop counter doubles each iteration, so after k steps it reaches 2^k. Setting 2^k = n gives k = log2(n), so the loop runs O(log n) times.
steps: Recognize the counter doubles, not increments.
Model the counter after k steps as 2^k.
Solve 2^k = n for k, giving k = log2(n).
Conclude the runtime is O(log n).

mistakes.mistake: Reporting O(2n) or O(n + 5) instead of simplifying to O(n).
mistakes.fix: Drop constant factors and lower-order terms; only the dominant term matters.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring space used by recursion call stacks or auxiliary structures.
mistakes.fix: Count extra memory besides the input, including stack frames in recursive solutions.

mistakes.mistake: Claiming a solution is O(n) because the input is sorted without justifying why.
mistakes.fix: Analyze the actual loop structure and state what assumption makes the bound hold.

problems.name: Finding the largest element
problems.description: Given an array of integers, return the maximum value. Analyze the runtime of scanning once.
hints: Scan every element exactly once and keep a running maximum.
How does the work scale as n doubles?
problems.approach: Iterate once over the array, updating a max variable whenever a larger value is seen.
problems.solution: Initialize result to negative infinity, loop through each element, update result if the current value is larger, and return result. One pass means linear work.

problems.name: Nested pair sum check
problems.description: Given an array, count how many pairs (i, j) with i < j exist. Analyze the complexity of the brute-force double loop.
hints: Write the double loop that visits every ordered pair.
Count the total number of pair visits in terms of n.
problems.approach: Run a nested loop where the inner loop starts after the outer index, producing roughly n^2/2 iterations.
problems.solution: The outer loop runs n times and the inner loop runs n-i-1 times, summing to n(n-1)/2, which is O(n^2).

problems.name: Binary search complexity
problems.description: Given a sorted array and a target, explain why binary search runs in logarithmic time and not linear time.
hints: Each comparison eliminates half of the remaining range.
How many times can you halve n before reaching one element?
problems.approach: Repeatedly halve the search interval, discarding the half that cannot contain the target.
problems.solution: Each step removes half the candidates, so the number of steps is the number of times n can be halved, which is log2(n).

name: Recursion
overview: Recursion solves a problem by breaking it into smaller copies of the same problem, calling a function on itself with a reduced input. A base case stops the calls, and a recursive case makes progress toward that base. It is the natural way to express tree, graph, and divide-and-conquer algorithms.
why: Recursion is pervasive in interview problems: trees, backtracking, permutations, and divide-and-conquer all rely on it. Many interviewers probe whether you can reason about a recursive call stack and its base cases.
when: Reach for recursion when a problem can be defined in terms of itself, such as traversing a tree, generating combinations, or computing values defined by a recurrence like factorials or Fibonacci.

complexity.time: Depends on branching factor and depth

concepts.name: Base case
concepts.description: The smallest input that returns an answer directly without another recursive call.

concepts.name: Recursive case
concepts.description: The branch that reduces the input and calls the function again.

concepts.name: Call stack
concepts.description: The runtime stack that holds each pending recursive call's local variables.

concepts.name: Stack depth
concepts.description: The number of nested calls, which bounds the extra memory recursion uses.

concepts.name: Divide and conquer
concepts.description: Splitting the problem into independent subproblems, solving each recursively, and combining results.

patterns.name: Simple recursion
patterns.description: Express a value in terms of a smaller version of itself.

patterns.name: Divide and conquer
patterns.description: Split input in half, solve each half recursively, merge results.

patterns.name: Backtracking skeleton
patterns.description: Build a partial solution, recurse, then undo the last choice.

examples.title: Fibonacci via recursion
examples.problem: Return the n-th Fibonacci number using recursion and identify the flaw in the naive version.
examples.explanation: fib(6) = fib(5) + fib(4) = 5 + 3 = 8. The naive recursion recomputes overlapping subproblems, giving exponential time, which is the key limitation to spot.
steps: Define fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1 as base cases.
Write the recurrence fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2).
Trace the overlapping subproblems such as fib(3) computed many times.
Note that memoization or iteration fixes the exponential blow-up.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the base case and hitting infinite recursion or a stack overflow.
mistakes.fix: Always write and test the base case first; ensure every call reduces the input.

mistakes.mistake: Redoing identical subproblems in naive recursion such as Fibonacci.
mistakes.fix: Add memoization with a dictionary or switch to an iterative bottom-up approach.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring stack depth, causing RecursionError on large inputs.
mistakes.fix: Convert deep recursion to iteration or an explicit stack when n is large.

problems.name: Factorial
problems.description: Given a non-negative integer n, return n! using recursion.
hints: What is the simplest input that returns directly?
Express n! in terms of (n-1)!.
problems.approach: Return 1 for n <= 1, otherwise return n times the factorial of n-1.
problems.solution: The base case returns 1, and the recursive case multiplies n by the result of calling the function on n-1, producing a chain of n calls.

problems.name: Generate all permutations
problems.description: Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible permutations.
hints: Pick one element to fix, then recurse on the rest.
How many leaves does the recursion tree have?
problems.approach: Choose each remaining element as the next in the permutation, recurse, and collect results when no elements remain.
problems.solution: At each step pick an unused element and recurse on the remainder. The recursion tree has n! leaves and building each permutation costs O(n) work.

problems.name: Power of four
problems.description: Given an integer n, return true if it is a power of four, false otherwise.
hints: What does dividing n by 4 repeatedly do?
What should the final value be if n is a power of four?
problems.approach: Recursively divide n by 4 as long as it is divisible and positive, then check the remainder.
problems.solution: If n is 1 it is a power of four. If n is not divisible by 4, return false. Otherwise recurse on n // 4 until reaching 1 or failing.

problems.name: Merge sort
problems.description: Sort an array using the divide-and-conquer merge sort algorithm.
hints: What is the base case for a trivially sorted slice?
How do you combine two sorted halves?
problems.approach: Split the array in half, recursively sort each half, and merge the two sorted halves in linear time.
problems.solution: Each level of the recursion splits the input, giving log n levels, and merging at each level costs O(n) total, so the total is O(n log n).

name: Basic mathematics for programming
overview: This topic covers the number-theoretic and arithmetic tools used in coding problems: gcd, lcm, modular arithmetic, primality, prime factorization, and fast exponentiation. These ideas appear constantly in leetcode-style questions and combinatorics.
why: Math problems are common interview filters, and math reasoning underlies combinatorial counting, probability, and DP problems. Knowing gcd, modular arithmetic, and prime-related algorithms lets you solve a whole class of otherwise intimidating questions.
when: Reach for these techniques when a problem mentions divisibility, remainders, prime numbers, huge exponents, or counting combinations. Modular arithmetic is essential whenever outputs could overflow or when exact division results matter.

complexity.time: Varies: O(sqrt(n)) primality, O(log n) gcd/exponentiation

concepts.name: GCD and LCM
concepts.description: Greatest common divisor and least common multiple; lcm(a,b) = a*b/gcd(a,b).

concepts.name: Modular arithmetic
concepts.description: Working with remainders mod m, where addition and multiplication wrap around.

concepts.name: Primality testing
concepts.description: Determining whether a number has no divisors besides 1 and itself, tested up to sqrt(n).

concepts.name: Prime factorization
concepts.description: Writing a number as a product of primes, used for divisors and lcm/gcd reasoning.

concepts.name: Fast exponentiation
concepts.description: Computing a^b in O(log b) time by squaring the base repeatedly.

concepts.name: Sieve of Eratosthenes
concepts.description: Marking multiples to list all primes up to a limit in near-linear time.

patterns.name: Euclidean algorithm
patterns.description: gcd via repeated remainder: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b).

patterns.name: Modular exponentiation
patterns.description: Exponentiation by squaring with a modulus applied at every step.

patterns.name: Primality by trial division
patterns.description: Check divisors only up to the square root of the number.

examples.title: Computing GCD
examples.problem: Find the greatest common divisor of 48 and 18 using the Euclidean algorithm.
examples.explanation: 48 % 18 = 12, then 18 % 12 = 6, then 12 % 6 = 0, so 6 divides both and is the gcd.
steps: The last nonzero remainder, 6, is the gcd.

mistakes.mistake: Using lcm(a,b) = a*b/gcd(a,b) naively and overflowing with big inputs.
mistakes.fix: Divide one value by the gcd first, then multiply: lcm = a // gcd(a, b) * b.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to apply the modulus after every multiplication in fast exponentiation.
mistakes.fix: Take mod at each step so intermediate values never grow huge.

mistakes.mistake: Testing primality by checking every number up to n instead of sqrt(n).
mistakes.fix: Only divisors up to sqrt(n) can exist, so stop the trial loop there.

problems.name: Greatest common divisor
problems.description: Given two integers a and b, return their greatest common divisor.
hints: What happens when you replace (a, b) with (b, a % b)?
What is the base case when one number is zero?
problems.approach: Repeatedly replace the larger pair by the remainder until one becomes zero.
problems.solution: Iteratively apply gcd(b, a % b) until b is zero, at which point a is the answer. Each step shrinks the numbers rapidly.

problems.name: Pow(x, n) mod m
problems.description: Given base x, exponent n, and modulus m, return x^n mod m efficiently.
hints: Express n in binary and square the base each step.
When is the current power multiplied into the result?
problems.approach: Exponentiation by squaring: process bits of the exponent and square the base each step.
problems.solution: Walk over the bits of n. If the bit is set, multiply the running result by the current base power, and square the base at every step while reducing mod m.

problems.name: Count primes
problems.description: Given an integer n, return the number of prime numbers strictly less than n.
hints: Start by assuming every number is prime and mark multiples.
From which number can you start marking to avoid redundant work?
problems.approach: Use the sieve of Eratosthenes: iterate numbers and mark their multiples as composite.
problems.solution: Build a boolean array of size n, mark every prime's multiples as composite starting from 2, then count remaining true entries.

problems.name: Perfect number
problems.description: Given an integer n, return true if n equals the sum of its proper positive divisors.
hints: Which divisors can you find without scanning to n?
How do you avoid double-counting the square root?
problems.approach: Find all divisors by scanning up to sqrt(n) and add the complementary divisor for each match.
problems.solution: For each i up to sqrt(n) that divides n, add both i and n/i to a sum, subtract n itself, and compare with n.

name: Bit manipulation
overview: Bit manipulation works directly on the binary representation of integers using operators like AND, OR, XOR, shifts, and bit masks. It enables extremely fast operations for counting bits, checking powers of two, toggling flags, and solving certain parity problems.
why: Bit tricks appear frequently as elegant one-liner solutions in interviews, such as detecting the single non-duplicate number or counting set bits. They also show comfort with low-level thinking that interviewers often reward.
when: Reach for bit manipulation when constraints involve 32-bit integers, when a problem asks about parity, toggling, masks, or when a brute-force set-based solution can be replaced by an XOR or bit-counting trick.

complexity.time: O(1) to O(bits) for word-sized ops

concepts.name: AND / OR / XOR
concepts.description: Per-bit logic operations; XOR is key for parity because a ^ a = 0.

concepts.name: Left shift
concepts.description: Shifts bits left, multiplying by powers of two: x << k equals x * 2^k.

concepts.name: Right shift
concepts.description: Shifts bits right, dividing by powers of two: x >> k equals floor(x / 2^k).

concepts.name: Bit masks
concepts.description: Integer patterns used with AND/OR to extract or set specific bits.

concepts.name: Power of two check
concepts.description: n is a power of two when n > 0 and n & (n - 1) == 0.

patterns.name: Count set bits
patterns.description: Clear the lowest set bit repeatedly using n &= n - 1.

patterns.name: Isolate lowest set bit
patterns.description: Extract the lowest set bit with n & -n (two's complement).
patterns.code:
def lowest(n):
    return n & -n

patterns.name: XOR single number
patterns.description: XOR all elements; paired values cancel to zero.

examples.title: Finding the single non-duplicate
examples.problem: Every element appears twice except one; find that single element using XOR.
examples.explanation: XOR is commutative and a ^ a = 0, so 1 ^ 1 and 2 ^ 2 cancel, leaving only 4.
steps: Initialize result to 0.
XOR each array element into result.
Identical pairs cancel because x ^ x = 0.
The remaining value is the unique element.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing up bitwise AND (&) with logical AND (and) in Python.
mistakes.fix: Use & for per-bit masks and and for boolean logic; the two are not interchangeable.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming negative numbers behave like positive ones in shifts.
mistakes.fix: Remember right shifts of negatives preserve the sign bit; prefer logical thinking on the non-negative range or mask the sign.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting operator precedence in expressions like n & n - 1.
mistakes.fix: Parenthesize: (n & (n - 1)) to avoid surprising precedence rules.

problems.name: Single number
problems.description: Given an array where every element appears twice except one, find the single element in linear time and constant space.
hints: What does x ^ x equal?
Can XORing everything reveal the unique value?
problems.approach: XOR all numbers; duplicates cancel, leaving the unique element.
problems.solution: XOR is associative and x ^ x = 0, so pairing duplicates collapse to zero and only the unique number remains.

problems.name: Power of two
problems.description: Given an integer n, return true if it is a power of two.
hints: A power of two has exactly one set bit.
What happens to the set bits when you compute n - 1?
problems.approach: A positive n is a power of two exactly when n & (n - 1) == 0.
problems.solution: Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit and everything below it, so n and n - 1 share no set bits only when n had exactly one.

problems.name: Number of 1 bits
problems.description: Given a non-negative integer, count its set bits (Hamming weight).
hints: What does n & (n - 1) remove?
How many times can you remove a set bit?
problems.approach: Repeatedly clear the lowest set bit with n &= n - 1 and count the iterations.
problems.solution: Each iteration of n &= n - 1 clears exactly one set bit, so the loop runs exactly as many times as there are ones.

problems.name: Missing number
problems.description: Given an array of n distinct numbers from 0 to n, find the missing one.
hints: XOR the index with the value at that index.
What cancels if a number matches its index?
problems.approach: XOR all indices 0..n together with every array value; matching pairs cancel, leaving the missing number.
problems.solution: XOR the complete range with the given values; each present value cancels its index, leaving the index that never appeared.

name: 1D/2D arrays
overview: Arrays are contiguous blocks of elements accessed by index; 2D arrays are grids of rows and columns, often used for matrices, tables, and graphs on a grid. Mastering traversal, boundaries, and in-place updates is the foundation of nearly every interview algorithm.
why: Arrays are the most common data structure in interviews, and 2D arrays appear in matrix traversal, DP, and graph problems. Almost every problem starts with correctly modeling the data as an array.
when: Reach for arrays whenever data is indexed, ordered, or grid-shaped. Use a 2D array when a problem describes rows and columns, matrices, or coordinates.

complexity.time: O(n) access by index, O(n^2) grid work

concepts.name: Indexing and bounds
concepts.description: Elements are accessed in O(1) by index, but you must stay within 0..n-1.

concepts.name: Row-major order
concepts.description: 2D arrays stored row by row; element (i, j) maps to i * cols + j.

concepts.name: In-place mutation
concepts.description: Modifying the array without allocating a new one, saving space.

concepts.name: Grid traversal
concepts.description: Moving up, down, left, right via direction arrays with bounds checks.

concepts.name: Slicing and copying
concepts.description: Extracting subarrays or cloning arrays; beware shallow copies of nested rows.

patterns.name: Directional traversal
patterns.description: Move on a grid using a delta array of steps.

patterns.name: Reverse in place
patterns.description: Swap elements from both ends toward the middle.

patterns.name: Transpose a matrix
patterns.description: Swap rows and columns using symmetric index swaps.

examples.title: Reverse an array in place
examples.problem: Reverse the order of elements in an array without allocating extra memory.
examples.explanation: Swap the first and last elements, then move inward. The middle element stays put when the length is odd.
steps: Set pointers at both ends of the array.
Swap the values at the two pointers.
Move the left pointer right and the right pointer left.
Stop when the pointers cross.

mistakes.mistake: Indexing out of bounds, especially in 2D loops where the inner bound uses the wrong dimension.
mistakes.fix: Use len(grid) for rows and len(grid[0]) for columns and verify bounds in every loop.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming a slice of a 2D array copies the inner rows.
mistakes.fix: Copy explicitly with [row[:] for row in grid] when mutation must not leak.

mistakes.mistake: Mutating an array while iterating over it, causing skipped or shifted elements.
mistakes.fix: Iterate over a copy or collect changes first, then apply them.

problems.name: Rotate array
problems.description: Rotate an array to the right by k steps in place.
hints: What happens if k is larger than the array length?
How many reversals does it take to rotate an array?
problems.approach: Reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k elements and the remaining n - k elements.
problems.solution: Normalize k modulo n. Reverse everything, reverse the first k, reverse the rest; the three reversals rotate the array in constant extra space.

problems.name: Transpose matrix
problems.description: Given a square matrix, transpose it in place by swapping rows and columns.
hints: Which pairs of cells must be swapped?
Why does the inner loop start at i + 1?
problems.approach: For each row i, swap cell (i, j) with (j, i) for j > i.
problems.solution: Each element above the main diagonal is swapped with its mirror below the diagonal, transposing the square matrix in place.

problems.name: Move zeroes
problems.description: Move all zeros in an array to the end while preserving the relative order of non-zero elements.
hints: Keep a write pointer for the next non-zero position.
What should happen to the cells after the last non-zero element?
problems.approach: Use a write pointer; copy each non-zero element forward, then fill the tail with zeros.
problems.solution: Walk the array with a write pointer, placing each non-zero at the pointer and advancing it. Afterwards, zero out all remaining positions.

problems.name: Matrix diagonal sum
problems.description: Given a square matrix, return the sum of the matrix diagonals without double-counting the center.
hints: What are the indices of the primary diagonal?
What about the secondary diagonal, and when does it overlap?
problems.approach: Sum cells where i == j for the main diagonal and i + j == n - 1 for the anti-diagonal, subtracting the center once for odd n.
problems.solution: Iterate rows once, adding the main diagonal element and the anti-diagonal element unless the same cell is counted twice when n is odd.

name: Prefix sum
overview: A prefix sum array stores the cumulative sum up to each index, so the sum of any subarray can be answered in constant time. Precompute once in O(n), then each range sum query is O(1).
why: Range-sum queries are a frequent sub-problem in interviews, and prefix sums underpin many medium problems on subarray sums. Demonstrating that subarray sums do not require re-scanning is a strong optimization signal.
when: Reach for prefix sums when you need many range sums over the same array, or when a problem asks whether some subarray equals a target sum. Extend to 2D prefix sums for rectangle sums on grids.

concepts.name: Prefix array
concepts.description: pref[i] holds the sum of the first i elements, making pref[j+1] - pref[i] the sum of a[i..j].

concepts.name: Subarray sum formula
concepts.description: sum(i..j) = pref[j+1] - pref[i], a single subtraction.

concepts.name: 2D prefix sum
concepts.description: A grid of cumulative sums that answers rectangle sums with inclusion-exclusion.

concepts.name: Zero-based vs one-based
concepts.description: Padding with a leading zero simplifies the difference formula and avoids index branches.

patterns.name: Build prefix sums
patterns.description: Accumulate running totals into an array.

patterns.name: Range sum query
patterns.description: Answer sum over a[i..j] with two array reads.
patterns.code:
def range_sum(pref, i, j):
    return pref[j + 1] - pref[i]

patterns.name: 2D prefix sum
patterns.description: Cumulative rectangle sums via inclusion-exclusion.

examples.title: Range sum query
examples.problem: Answer the sum of elements from index 1 to 3 of [2, 4, 1, 7, 3].
examples.explanation: Prefix sums are [0, 2, 6, 7, 14, 17]. The range sum is pref[4] - pref[1] = 14 - 2 = 12, matching 4 + 1 + 7.
steps: Build the prefix array [0, 2, 6, 7, 14, 17].
Use the formula sum(i..j) = pref[j+1] - pref[i].
Substitute i = 1 and j = 3 to get 14 - 2.
Return 12 in constant time.

complexity.time: O(1) per query after O(n) build

mistakes.mistake: Off-by-one errors between pref indices and array indices.
mistakes.fix: Store prefix of length n + 1 with pref[0] = 0 so range i..j maps to pref[j+1] - pref[i].

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to handle empty subarrays or negative sums in formulas.
mistakes.fix: Define the answer in terms of a difference of prefix values and let the leading zero absorb empty cases.

mistakes.mistake: Rebuilding the prefix array inside each query instead of once.
mistakes.fix: Precompute once up front; queries should only read the array.

problems.name: Range sum query - immutable
problems.description: Design a structure that answers sum(i..j) queries on an immutable array in constant time.
hints: What should the constructor precompute?
How do you turn two prefix values into a range sum?
problems.approach: Precompute a prefix sum array in the constructor and answer each query with one subtraction.
problems.solution: The constructor builds pref where pref[i] is the sum of the first i elements. Each query returns pref[right+1] - pref[left].

problems.name: Subarray sum equals K
problems.description: Given an integer array and an integer k, count subarrays whose sum equals k.
hints: How can prefix sums express a subarray sum?
What should you look up in a hash map as you scan?
problems.approach: Track running prefix sums in a hash map; a subarray ending at i sums to k when a previous prefix equals current - k.
problems.solution: As you build running sums, record counts of each prefix. For each new prefix, add the count of prefixes equal to prefix - k to the answer.

problems.name: Range sum query 2D - immutable
problems.description: Design a structure that answers sums of rectangular submatrices in constant time.
hints: Build cumulative sums for the whole grid.
Which three rectangles must be subtracted from the big one?
problems.approach: Precompute a 2D prefix array and answer each rectangle query with inclusion-exclusion.
problems.solution: Rectangle sum from (r1,c1) to (r2,c2) is p[r2+1][c2+1] - p[r1][c2+1] - p[r2+1][c1] + p[r1][c1].

problems.name: Contiguous array
problems.description: Given a binary array, find the longest contiguous subarray with an equal number of zeros and ones.
hints: Treat zeros as -1 and find the longest subarray summing to zero.
When do two equal prefix sums imply a zero-sum subarray?
problems.approach: Map zeros to -1, record the first occurrence of each prefix sum, and find the farthest repeat.
problems.solution: A subarray has equal zeros and ones iff its sum is zero. Track the first index where each prefix sum appeared; equal prefixes bracket a zero-sum subarray.

name: Difference arrays
overview: A difference array stores the change between consecutive elements, so adding a constant to a contiguous range becomes just two updates. It is the dual of the prefix sum and converts range-add operations from O(n) per query to O(1) per query with one final prefix pass.
why: Range-update problems appear in interviews as sweep-line or calendar-style questions, and difference arrays turn otherwise quadratic solutions into linear ones. Recognizing the pattern shows strong command of array techniques.
when: Reach for a difference array when you apply many range additions to an array and then read the final values. It is also used in interval overlap counting such as booking schedules.

complexity.time: O(1) per range update, O(n) finalize

concepts.name: Difference array
concepts.description: diff[i] = arr[i] - arr[i-1]; summing diff recovers arr.

concepts.name: Range add
concepts.description: Adding v to arr[l..r] is diff[l] += v and diff[r+1] -= v.

concepts.name: Reconstruction
concepts.description: One prefix-sum pass over diff recovers the final array.

concepts.name: Interval overlap
concepts.description: Adding +1 over an interval and reading the running total counts how many intervals cover each point.

patterns.name: Range add
patterns.description: Encode a range increment as two diff updates.

patterns.name: Reconstruct array
patterns.description: Prefix-sum the diff array to recover final values.
patterns.code:
def build(diff):
    cur = 0
    res = []
    for d in diff:
        cur += d
        res.append(cur)
    return res

examples.title: Range additions
examples.problem: Start with an array of five zeros and add 3 to indices 1..3 and 2 to indices 2..4.
examples.explanation: First add bumps diff[1] and diff[4]; second bumps diff[2] and diff[5]. Prefix-summing yields the final values: 0, 3, 5, 5, 2.
steps: Initialize diff of length 6 to zeros.
Prefix-sum diff over the first 5 entries to get the result.

mistakes.mistake: Applying the subtract at diff[r] instead of diff[r+1], corrupting every later element.
mistakes.fix: The range add l..r must subtract at index r+1 so the increment stops after r.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to allocate an extra slot for the r+1 update.
mistakes.fix: Size the diff array as n + 1 (or longer) so the closing update never goes out of bounds.

mistakes.mistake: Treating diff values as the final array without the prefix pass.
mistakes.fix: Always reconstruct by accumulating; diff only stores deltas, not values.

problems.name: Range addition
problems.description: Given length n and a list of updates (start, end, inc), return the final array after all updates.
hints: What two positions change per update?
How do you rebuild the array from the deltas?
problems.approach: Apply each range update to a difference array, then prefix-sum to get the result.
problems.solution: For each update add inc at diff[start] and subtract it at diff[end+1]. A single prefix pass over diff produces the final array.

problems.name: Corporate flight bookings
problems.description: Given n flights and bookings in (first, last, seats), return how many seats are booked per flight.
hints: Each booking is a range addition over flight indices.
Can you use a difference array over the n flights?
problems.approach: Treat each booking as a range add and apply all bookings to a difference array over the flights.
problems.solution: For each booking, add seats at diff[first-1] and subtract at diff[last]. Prefix-summing yields the seat counts per flight.

problems.name: Meeting rooms
problems.description: Given a list of time intervals [start, end], find the maximum number of overlapping meetings at any moment.
hints: How can a difference array count active meetings over time?
What is the answer after reconstructing the running totals?
problems.approach: Use a difference array over time points, adding +1 at each start and -1 at each end, then take the max running total.
problems.time: O(T + n) where T is the time span
problems.solution: Increment at every start and decrement at every end in a diff array sized to the max time. Prefix-sum and track the maximum active count.

name: Two pointers
overview: The two-pointer technique uses two indices moving through an array, usually from both ends or at different speeds, to solve problems in a single pass. It exploits monotonicity or ordering to avoid nested loops and is a key linear-time tool for sorted arrays.
why: Two pointers is one of the most frequently tested patterns and often converts an O(n^2) brute force into O(n). Interviewers expect it for problems on sorted arrays, palindrome checks, and sum targets.
when: Reach for two pointers when the input is sorted, when you need to find pairs that satisfy a condition, or when a naive double loop feels wasteful. The pattern works whenever moving one pointer preserves the answer's feasibility region.

concepts.name: Opposite-direction pointers
concepts.description: One pointer at each end moving inward toward a meeting point, as in two-sum on a sorted array.

concepts.name: Same-direction pointers
concepts.description: A slow and fast pointer, or left/right both advancing forward, as in removing duplicates.

concepts.name: Monotonic window
concepts.description: Since the array is ordered, moving a pointer only ever enlarges or shrinks the candidate set.

concepts.name: Termination
concepts.description: The loop ends when the pointers meet or the fast pointer exhausts the array.

patterns.name: Two sum sorted
patterns.description: Shrink from both ends to find a target sum.

patterns.name: Remove duplicates in place
patterns.description: Write unique values forward with a write pointer.

patterns.name: Two-pointer palindrome
patterns.description: Compare characters from both ends toward the center.

examples.title: Two sum in a sorted array
examples.problem: Given a sorted array, find two numbers that add up to a target.
examples.explanation: Start with 1 + 8 = 9 which already matches. Moving inward with the left pointer increases the sum and the right pointer decreases it, so the correct pair is found in one pass.
steps: Place left at 0 and right at the last index.
If the sum equals the target, return the pair.
If the sum is too small, move left right.
If the sum is too large, move right left.

mistakes.mistake: Using two pointers on an unsorted array and expecting the monotonic logic to hold.
mistakes.fix: Sort the array first, or use a hash map if order must be preserved.

mistakes.mistake: Letting the loop run past the pointers crossing and double-counting pairs.
mistakes.fix: Use strict i < j as the loop condition so each pair is considered once.

mistakes.mistake: Moving the wrong pointer when sums are equal to the target.
mistakes.fix: Return immediately on equality; only advance when the sum is strictly below or above.

problems.name: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
problems.description: Given a 1-indexed sorted array, find two numbers that sum to the target and return their 1-based indices.
hints: Why is the sorted property essential for this approach?
When should each pointer move?
problems.approach: Place pointers at both ends and adjust based on the current sum relative to the target.
problems.solution: If the sum is below the target the left pointer moves right; if above, the right pointer moves left; equal sums are returned.

problems.name: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
problems.description: Remove duplicates in place from a sorted array and return the new length.
hints: Where does each unique value belong?
When should the write pointer advance?
problems.approach: Walk with a read pointer and a write pointer that only advances when a new distinct value appears.
problems.solution: Each element different from the last written value is copied forward and the write pointer advances; the final write pointer is the new length.

problems.name: Valid Palindrome
problems.description: Check if a string is a palindrome, ignoring case and non-alphanumeric characters.
hints: Which characters should be skipped?
What happens when both pointers land on letters?
problems.approach: Use two pointers from both ends, skipping non-alphanumerics, and compare the remaining letters case-insensitively.
problems.solution: Advance each pointer past invalid characters, then compare the letters in lowercase; any mismatch means it is not a palindrome.

problems.name: Container With Most Water
problems.description: Given heights, find two lines that form a container holding the most water.
hints: Which pointer determines the water level?
Can a shorter outer line ever be the better boundary?
problems.approach: Start pointers at both ends, compute the area, and always move the pointer with the shorter height inward.
problems.solution: The area is limited by the shorter line. Moving the taller pointer can only shrink the width without raising the limit, so always move the shorter side and track the max area.

name: Sliding window
overview: A sliding window maintains a contiguous subarray or substring whose boundaries move as you scan, keeping a running value that is updated when elements enter and leave the window. It converts many nested-loop substring problems into a single linear pass.
why: Sliding window is one of the highest-frequency patterns for substring and subarray problems in interviews. It is the standard tool for longest/substring constraints and for finding subarrays meeting sum or product bounds.
when: Reach for a sliding window when a problem asks for a contiguous subarray or substring satisfying a condition, especially with keywords like longest, shortest, or maximum under a constraint.

concepts.name: Window boundaries
concepts.description: Left and right pointers define the current contiguous segment; right expands, left shrinks.

concepts.name: Window invariant
concepts.description: A condition the window must satisfy, such as all characters distinct or sum at most k.

concepts.name: Expand and shrink
concepts.description: Extend right until the invariant breaks, then advance left until it holds again.

concepts.name: Fixed vs variable size
concepts.description: Fixed windows move in lockstep; variable windows grow and shrink to satisfy a condition.

patterns.name: Longest substring no repeats
patterns.description: Shrink from the left until repeated chars are removed.

patterns.name: Fixed window sum
patterns.description: Slide a window of size k and update the sum incrementally.
patterns.code:
def max_sum(a, k):
    cur = sum(a[:k])
    best = cur
    for i in range(k, len(a)):
        cur += a[i] - a[i - k]
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best

patterns.name: Variable window with condition
patterns.description: Shrink the left pointer until the condition holds again.
patterns.code:
def longest_with_sum_at_most(a, k):
    left = 0
    cur = 0
    best = 0
    for right, x in enumerate(a):
        cur += x
        while cur > k:
            cur -= a[left]
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

examples.title: Maximum sum of a fixed window
examples.problem: Find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of size k.
examples.explanation: Windows are [2,1,5]=8, [1,5,1]=7, [5,1,3]=9, [1,3,2]=6; the max is 9. Each new window only adds one element and removes one.
steps: Sum the first k elements as the initial window.
Slide right one step, adding the new element.
Subtract the element that left the window.
Track the maximum window sum seen.

mistakes.mistake: Using a while loop that re-scans the window instead of updating incrementally.
mistakes.fix: Add the incoming element and subtract the outgoing one so each step is O(1).

mistakes.mistake: Shrinking the window too far or not far enough when the invariant breaks.
mistakes.fix: Advance left exactly until the invariant is restored, then continue expanding right.

mistakes.mistake: Applying the technique when the condition is not monotonic in the window.
mistakes.fix: Verify that growing the window always worsens the condition, or use a different approach.

problems.name: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.description: Given a string, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
hints: When you see a repeated character, where should the window restart?
How do you remember the last position of each character?
problems.approach: Slide a window and keep the last seen index of each character; on a repeat, jump the left boundary past the duplicate.
problems.solution: Maintain a map of the last position of each char. When a char repeats within the window, move left to just after its previous occurrence, and update the max length.

problems.name: Maximum Average Subarray I
problems.description: Find a contiguous subarray of size k with the maximum average value.
hints: Which subarray of fixed size maximizes the average?
How do you update the sum as the window slides?
problems.approach: Slide a fixed-size window and track the maximum sum, then divide by k.
problems.solution: Compute the sum of the first k elements, then for each slide add the new element and subtract the one leaving, keeping the maximum sum.

problems.name: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
problems.description: Find the minimal length of a contiguous subarray whose sum is at least the target.
hints: When the sum exceeds the target, what should you do?
Can shrinking the left side produce a shorter valid window?
problems.approach: Expand the right pointer until the sum reaches the target, then shrink from the left while the sum stays valid.
problems.solution: Grow the window until the sum is at least target, then shrink left while it remains at least target, tracking the shortest window length.

problems.name: Permutation in String
problems.description: Check whether one string contains a permutation of another as a substring.
hints: What does a permutation window look like in character counts?
How can a fixed-size sliding window validate the counts?
problems.approach: Compare character frequency counts of a fixed-size window in s2 against the counts of s1.
problems.solution: Count characters of s1, slide a window of that length over s2, updating counts and checking equality against the target counts.

name: Kadane's algorithm
overview: Kadane's algorithm finds the maximum sum of a contiguous subarray in a single linear pass. It keeps a running best sum ending at the current element and resets it to zero (or the element itself) whenever the running sum becomes negative.
why: Maximum subarray is one of the most classic interview problems, and Kadane's algorithm is the canonical O(n) solution every interviewer expects you to know cold. Its greedy reset idea generalizes to many DP-style subarray problems.
when: Reach for Kadane when a problem asks for the maximum-sum contiguous subarray, or maximum product with a twist, and the array can contain negative numbers.

concepts.name: Running best ending here
concepts.description: The maximum sum of a subarray ending exactly at the current index.

concepts.name: Reset on negative
concepts.description: If the running sum drops below the current element, a fresh subarray from here is better.

concepts.name: Global best
concepts.description: The maximum over all running bests seen so far, which is the final answer.

concepts.name: Extension to 2D
concepts.description: Combining prefix columns with Kadane solves maximum rectangle sum in O(n^2 * m).

patterns.name: Classic Kadane
patterns.description: Linear scan keeping the best subarray sum ending here.

patterns.name: Kadane with reset to zero
patterns.description: Reset the running sum to zero whenever it is negative.

patterns.name: Maximum circular subarray
patterns.description: Handle wrap-around using total minus minimum subarray sum.

examples.title: Maximum subarray
examples.problem: Find the maximum sum of a contiguous subarray.
examples.explanation: The subarray [4, -1, 2, 1] sums to 6. Kadane finds it because starting fresh at 4 beats carrying the negative prefix -2 + 1 - 3 = -4.
steps: Initialize best and cur to the first element.
For each next element, set cur = max(x, cur + x).
Update best = max(best, cur).
Return best, which is 6 for this input.

mistakes.mistake: Initializing best to 0, which fails when all elements are negative.
mistakes.fix: Initialize best and cur to the first element so a single negative value is still a valid answer.

mistakes.mistake: Resetting cur to 0 unconditionally instead of comparing with cur + x.
mistakes.fix: Use cur = max(x, cur + x) so an element larger than the running sum starts a fresh subarray.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting that the subarray must be contiguous when reading the problem.
mistakes.fix: If elements may be skipped, this is subset-sum, not Kadane; confirm contiguity first.

problems.name: Maximum Subarray
problems.description: Given an integer array, find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum.
hints: What is the best subarray ending at the current element?
When should you discard the running sum and start fresh?
problems.approach: Scan once, keeping the best sum ending at the current element as either the element alone or the element plus the previous best.
problems.solution: cur = max(x, cur + x) tracks the best subarray ending here, and best tracks the overall maximum, which is the answer.

problems.name: Maximum Product Subarray
problems.description: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest product.
hints: Why must you also track the minimum product?
How do negatives flip the roles of min and max?
problems.approach: Track both the maximum and minimum product ending at the current element, because a negative times the minimum becomes the new maximum.
problems.solution: Maintain cur_max and cur_min; at each element compute the three-way candidates including the element times the previous max and min, then update the global best.

problems.name: Maximum Sum Circular Subarray
problems.description: Find the maximum sum of a contiguous subarray in a circular array.
hints: When does the best subarray wrap around the ends?
How is the wrapped case related to the minimum subarray?
problems.approach: Compute the straight maximum subarray and the wrapped case as total minus the minimum subarray sum.
problems.solution: The answer is the max of the ordinary maximum subarray and total minus the minimum subarray; special-case when every element is negative.

problems.name: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
problems.description: Given daily prices, find the maximum profit from buying then selling on later days.
hints: What should you track as you scan the prices?
Can this be reduced to a max difference over a running minimum?
problems.approach: Track the minimum price seen so far and the best profit of selling on the current day.
problems.solution: Keep the lowest price seen and update profit with price - min_price each day; this is Kadane on the daily differences without materializing them.

name: Sorting-based problems
overview: Sorting-based problems treat sorting as a preprocessing step that simplifies the remaining work, such as turning searches into binary search or grouping equal elements together. After sorting, many O(n^2) problems become O(n log n) or O(n).
why: Sorting is a universal assumption in interview problems, and mentioning a sort-based approach shows you can trade O(n log n) preprocessing for simpler logic. Many problems explicitly expect a sort-first strategy.
when: Reach for sorting when a problem does not specify order but grouping, ranking, or nearest-neighbor comparisons would help. Sort when you need the k-th largest, intervals that can be merged, or pairs whose difference matters.

complexity.time: O(n log n) for the sort plus subsequent pass

concepts.name: Sorting as preprocessing
concepts.description: Ordering input so later comparisons, searches, or groupings become trivial.

concepts.name: Comparator and key functions
concepts.description: Custom orderings via keys or comparators for tuples, intervals, or strings.

concepts.name: Stability
concepts.description: Preserving relative order of equal elements, useful for multi-key sorts.

concepts.name: Two-pointer after sort
concepts.description: Sorted arrays enable the linear two-pointer search patterns for sums and differences.

patterns.name: Sort then two pointers
patterns.description: Sort the array and use opposite-direction pointers.

patterns.name: Sort by start then merge intervals
patterns.description: Order by start time and merge overlapping ranges in one pass.

patterns.name: Sort for k-th element
patterns.description: Sort once and pick the k-th index directly.

examples.title: Merge intervals
examples.problem: Merge all overlapping intervals in a list of [start, end] pairs.
examples.explanation: After sorting by start, [1,3] and [2,6] overlap because 2 <= 3, so they merge into [1,6]. [8,10] starts after 6, so it begins a new interval.
steps: Sort intervals by their start value.
Start an output list with the first interval.
For each interval, if its start exceeds the last end, append it.
Otherwise extend the last interval's end to the max.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming sorting is always O(n) or forgetting the sort dominates the complexity.
mistakes.fix: State the full complexity as O(n log n) when a sort is part of the solution.

mistakes.mistake: Sorting by the wrong field for interval problems.
mistakes.fix: For merging, sort by start; for greedy interval selection, sort by end.

mistakes.mistake: Using an unstable sort where tie-breaking between equal keys matters.
mistakes.fix: Add a secondary key or use a stable sort to preserve intended ordering.

problems.name: Merge Intervals
problems.description: Given an array of intervals, merge all overlapping intervals.
hints: What order makes overlaps easy to detect?
When do you extend the current interval versus start a new one?
problems.approach: Sort by start time, then scan and merge intervals that overlap with the current one.
problems.pattern: Sort by start then merge intervals
problems.solution: Sort by start, then for each interval either merge into the current one (extending its end) or push a new interval when it is disjoint.

problems.name: 3Sum
problems.description: Find all unique triplets in an array that sum to zero.
hints: How does sorting help avoid duplicate triplets?
Can two pointers solve the pair-sum for each fixed element?
problems.approach: Sort, fix one element, and run two pointers over the rest to find pairs summing to its negation, skipping duplicates.
problems.solution: For each i, run two pointers from i+1 to the end seeking the pair summing to -nums[i]; skip equal values to avoid duplicate triplets.

problems.name: Kth Largest Element in an Array
problems.description: Return the k-th largest element in an unsorted array.
hints: What index holds the k-th largest after sorting?
Could a heap do this with less than a full sort?
problems.approach: Sort descending and pick index k-1, or maintain a min-heap of size k.
problems.solution: Sorting descending makes the k-th largest the element at index k-1; a heap-based alternative keeps only the top k elements.

problems.name: Non-overlapping Intervals
problems.description: Find the minimum number of intervals to remove so the rest do not overlap.
hints: Which interval should be kept when two overlap?
What does sorting by end time buy you?
problems.approach: Sort by end time, greedily keep the interval that finishes earliest and count removals when overlaps occur.
problems.pattern: Sort by start then merge intervals
problems.solution: Sort by end. Always keep the earliest-finishing interval; whenever the next starts before the kept one ends, count it for removal.

name: String manipulation
overview: String manipulation covers building, splitting, reversing, and transforming strings while respecting immutability and encoding. Strings are immutable in Python, so transforms typically create new strings, and character-by-character scans are the heart of most string algorithms.
why: String problems are a large share of interview questions, from palindrome checks to anagram detection to word reversals. Comfort with char arrays, joins, and index math separates clean solutions from messy ones.
when: Reach for string manipulation when a problem involves ordering characters, splitting on delimiters, reversing words, or transforming text. Pair it with hashing when comparison must ignore ordering.

complexity.time: O(n) for single scans and joins

concepts.name: Immutability
concepts.description: Strings cannot be modified in place; rebuilding produces a new string.

concepts.name: Join and split
concepts.description: Split a string on delimiters and rejoin pieces efficiently with ''.join.

concepts.name: Character indexing
concepts.description: Accessing characters by position and slicing substrings in O(length).

concepts.name: Reversal
concepts.description: Reversing a whole string or reversing the order of words without reversing letters.

concepts.name: Case and normalization
concepts.description: Lowercasing and stripping non-alphanumerics to make comparisons uniform.

patterns.name: Reverse words in a sentence
patterns.description: Split on spaces, reverse the list, and rejoin.
patterns.code:
def reverse_words(s):
    return ' '.join(reversed(s.split()))

patterns.name: Build a char list then swap
patterns.description: Mutable work via a list of characters.

patterns.name: Compress by runs
patterns.description: Scan once and count consecutive runs of characters.

examples.title: Reverse words in a sentence
examples.problem: Reverse the order of words in a sentence while preserving each word's letters.
examples.explanation: Split on whitespace into ['the','sky','is','blue'], reverse the list, then join with single spaces.
steps: Split the input on whitespace to get words.
Reverse the resulting list in place.
Join the reversed words with a single space.
Return the joined string.

mistakes.mistake: Attempting in-place edits on an immutable string, causing TypeErrors.
mistakes.fix: Convert to a list, edit, then join, or build a new string with concatenation.

mistakes.mistake: Building strings with += in a loop, which is quadratic.
mistakes.fix: Collect pieces in a list and use ''.join once.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring multiple spaces or leading/trailing spaces when splitting words.
mistakes.fix: Use s.split() which handles all whitespace runs, instead of splitting on a single space.

problems.name: Reverse Words in a String
problems.description: Reverse the order of words in a string while removing extra spaces.
hints: How does split() normalize whitespace?
What does joining the reversed words give you?
problems.approach: Split on whitespace, reverse the words, and join with single spaces.
problems.solution: s.split() splits on any whitespace and drops empties, reversed() gives reverse order, and join restores a clean single-spaced sentence.

problems.name: Reverse String
problems.description: Reverse a string in place by treating it as an array of characters.
hints: Which two positions get swapped first?
When do the pointers stop?
problems.approach: Use two pointers from both ends, swapping characters until they meet.
problems.pattern: Build a char list then swap
problems.solution: Swap the characters at symmetric positions working inward from both ends until the pointers cross.

problems.name: Valid Anagram
problems.description: Check whether two strings are anagrams, containing the same characters with the same counts.
hints: What must be equal for two strings to be anagrams?
Can sorting make the comparison trivial?
problems.approach: Sort both strings and compare, or count character frequencies and compare the counts.
problems.time: O(n log n) sorted, O(n) with counting
problems.solution: Two strings are anagrams iff their sorted forms are identical, or equivalently iff their character frequency maps match.

problems.name: Longest Palindromic Substring
problems.description: Find the longest substring that reads the same forward and backward.
hints: Can you expand around the center of a palindrome?
What are the two possible center shapes?
problems.approach: Expand around every possible center, handling both odd-length and even-length palindromes.
problems.pattern: Build a char list then swap
problems.solution: For each center, grow outward while characters match, tracking the longest palindrome; try both single-char and two-char centers.

name: Frequency counting / hashing
overview: Frequency counting records how many times each distinct value appears, typically in a hash map or counter. It is the fastest way to answer questions about duplicates, most common elements, and whether multisets match.
why: Counting frequencies is the backbone of a huge family of interview problems: anagrams, majority elements, and duplicate detection. Interviewers love seeing a clean Counter-based solution where a naive approach would be quadratic.
when: Reach for frequency counting when you need the count of each distinct element, the most or least frequent element, or a quick equality check between multisets.

concepts.name: Frequency map
concepts.description: A dictionary mapping each distinct element to how many times it appears.

concepts.name: Counter as a multiset
concepts.description: Two collections are equal as multisets iff their frequency maps match.

concepts.name: Mode and majority
concepts.description: Finding the most frequent element or an element appearing more than n/2 times.

concepts.name: Negative vs positive counts
concepts.description: Using a single counter with increments and decrements to compare two multisets.

patterns.name: Build a counter
patterns.description: Count occurrences of each element in one pass.

patterns.name: Anagram check by counts
patterns.description: Build a counter, subtract, and verify all zeros.

patterns.name: Most frequent element
patterns.description: Scan the counter to find the element with the highest count.

examples.title: Finding the mode
examples.problem: Given an array, find the element that appears most frequently.
examples.explanation: Counting yields 3 appearing three times, more than any other value. A single pass to count and a second pass to select gives the answer.
steps: Initialize an empty frequency dictionary.
Increment the count of each element while scanning.
After the pass, scan the dictionary for the max count.
Return the element with the highest count.

mistakes.mistake: Using a list of size equal to the value range when values are large or negative.
mistakes.fix: Use a dictionary or Counter; array-based counting only fits small non-negative ranges.

mistakes.mistake: Mutating a dictionary while iterating over its items.
mistakes.fix: Iterate over a copy or collect keys first, then update.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting that frequency maps must handle missing keys on lookup.
mistakes.fix: Use freq.get(key, 0) so absent keys behave as zero without raising KeyError.

problems.name: Majority Element
problems.description: Find the element that appears more than n/2 times in an array.
hints: What is the count threshold for majority?
Can a single counter tell you the answer as you scan?
problems.approach: Count frequencies in a map and return any element whose count exceeds n/2, or use Boyer-Moore voting.
problems.solution: Build a frequency map and return the key with count above n/2. The Boyer-Moore variant achieves this in O(1) space.

problems.name: Valid Anagram
problems.description: Check if two strings contain exactly the same characters in the same counts.
hints: What does it mean for two strings to share a frequency map?
How can decrementing detect a mismatch early?
problems.approach: Count one string, then subtract the characters of the other and verify the counts never go negative.
problems.solution: Build a counter for s, then for each char of t decrement; a negative count or leftover positive count means the strings differ.

problems.name: Top K Frequent Elements
problems.description: Given an array, return the k most frequently occurring elements in any order.
hints: What structure gives you counts per element first?
How do you extract the top k from the counts?
problems.approach: Count frequencies, then use a heap or bucket sort over the counts to pick the top k.
problems.solution: Build frequency counts, then push (count, element) into a min-heap of size k, or bucket elements by frequency and scan from the top.

problems.name: Ransom Note
problems.description: Determine whether a magazine string can construct a ransom note using its letters.
hints: Which counts must the magazine satisfy?
When can you early-return false?
problems.approach: Count magazine letters, then consume them while building the note and fail if any letter runs out.
problems.solution: Count each letter in the magazine; for each note letter decrement its count and return false if it drops below zero.

name: Arrays & Strings
overview: Arrays and strings form the foundational data structures of most interview problems. Strings are effectively character arrays, so the techniques that work on arrays - indexing, two pointers, sliding windows, prefix sums - transfer directly with small adaptations for immutability and encoding.
why: A large fraction of interview questions are framed as array or string problems, and mastering this category first builds the confidence and toolkit for trees, graphs, and DP. Interviewers often use array-string questions to gauge basics quickly.
when: Reach for this category whenever data is ordered and indexed, whether it is a list of numbers or a string of characters. Most entry-level and mid-level problems fall into this bucket.

concepts.name: Indexing
concepts.description: O(1) random access by position, with strict bounds checking.

concepts.name: Contiguity
concepts.description: Arrays store elements in adjacent memory; strings are ordered character sequences.

concepts.name: String immutability
concepts.description: String transforms create new strings; mutable work requires char lists.

concepts.name: Subarray vs subsequence
concepts.description: Subarrays are contiguous slices; subsequences skip elements while preserving order.

concepts.name: Shared techniques
concepts.description: Two pointers, sliding windows, and prefix sums all apply to both arrays and strings.

patterns.name: Scan and accumulate
patterns.description: Single pass computing a running value such as a sum or max.

patterns.name: Compare from both ends
patterns.description: Mirror checks using two pointers, common for strings.
patterns.code:
def palindrome_pairs(a):
    return all(a[i] == a[-1 - i] for i in range(len(a) // 2))

patterns.name: In-place overwrite
patterns.description: Reuse the front of the array to compact or transform data.

examples.title: Single-pass best value
examples.problem: Find the maximum value in an integer array.
examples.explanation: Initialize best to the first element and update whenever a larger value appears. The answer after one pass is 10.
steps: Set best to the first element.
Visit each remaining element.
Update best when the element is larger.
Return best after the scan.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing a subsequence with a subarray and solving the wrong problem.
mistakes.fix: Check whether elements must be contiguous; subarray problems often use sliding windows or prefix sums.

mistakes.mistake: Mutating a string as if it were mutable.
mistakes.fix: Work with a character list or build new strings, then join at the end.

mistakes.mistake: Off-by-one errors when converting between 1-based problem statements and 0-based indexing.
mistakes.fix: Pin down the mapping early and test boundaries like the first and last elements.

problems.name: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
problems.description: Given daily prices, find the maximum profit from one buy and one later sell.
hints: What running value makes each day's profit easy to compute?
Can one pass track both the min price and the best profit?
problems.approach: Track the minimum price seen so far and the best profit achievable at each step.
problems.solution: For each price, the best profit is price minus the minimum seen so far; keep the overall maximum across all days.

problems.name: Two Sum
problems.description: Given an array and a target, return the indices of two numbers that add up to the target.
hints: What complement do you look for as you scan?
What data structure stores seen values and their indices?
problems.approach: Scan once, storing each value's index in a hash map and checking for the complement.
problems.solution: For each element, check whether target minus the element was seen before; if so return both indices, otherwise record the element.

problems.name: Contains Duplicate
problems.description: Determine if an array contains any duplicate elements.
hints: What happens when you insert a value into a set twice?
Can sorting detect duplicates more simply?
problems.approach: Insert each element into a set and return false on the first repeat.
problems.solution: Track seen values in a set; if an element is already present, a duplicate exists.

problems.name: First Unique Character in a String
problems.description: Find the index of the first character in a string that does not repeat.
hints: What two passes over the string do you need?
How do you know a character is unique after the first pass?
problems.approach: Count character frequencies in one pass, then scan again for the first character with count 1.
problems.solution: First pass builds a frequency map; second pass returns the index of the first character whose count is exactly 1.

name: Hashing
overview: Hashing maps keys to array slots using a hash function, giving near-constant-time insert, lookup, and delete on average. Hash maps and sets trade a bit of extra memory for dramatic speedups, turning many O(n^2) scans into O(n) lookups.
why: Hash maps are the single most used data structure in interviews, showing up in two-sum, anagram, frequency, and deduplication problems. Using hashing well signals that you can trade space for time deliberately.
when: Reach for hashing whenever you need fast membership tests, value lookups by key, or frequency counts. Use a hash set for uniqueness and a hash map when each key must carry associated data.

concepts.name: Hash function
concepts.description: A function mapping a key to an integer index within a fixed-size table.

concepts.name: Collision
concepts.description: Two distinct keys landing on the same slot; handled by chaining or open addressing.

concepts.name: Load factor
concepts.description: The ratio of stored items to table size; growing the table when it is high keeps lookups fast.

concepts.name: Set vs map
concepts.description: A set stores unique keys; a map stores key-value pairs for retrieval.

concepts.name: Average vs worst case
concepts.description: Operations are O(1) on average; adversarial keys can degrade to O(n).

patterns.name: Two-sum scan
patterns.description: Store complements and look them up while scanning.

patterns.name: Deduplicate with a set
patterns.description: Reject elements already seen.

patterns.name: Group by key
patterns.description: Bucket values under a computed key.

examples.title: Two-sum with a hash map
examples.problem: Find two array elements whose values add up to a target and return their indices.
examples.explanation: Scanning, 2 is stored. When 7 is reached, its complement 2 is already in the map, so indices 0 and 1 are returned in one pass.
steps: Initialize an empty dictionary mapping value to index.
For each element compute the complement target - x.
If the complement is stored, return both indices.
Otherwise store the current element with its index.

mistakes.mistake: Treating hashing as O(1) worst case instead of average case.
mistakes.fix: State 'expected O(1)' per operation and note the worst-case O(n) possibility under collisions.

mistakes.mistake: Using an array of size max-value for sparse or negative keys.
mistakes.fix: Prefer a dictionary; array indexing is only viable for dense non-negative small ranges.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting that tuples are hashable but lists are not.
mistakes.fix: Use tuples for compound keys and lists only as stored values.

problems.name: Two Sum
problems.description: Return the indices of two numbers that add up to a target, assuming exactly one solution.
hints: What complement do you search for at each step?
Where do you record each value as you go?
problems.approach: Single pass storing value-to-index in a hash map and checking complements.
problems.solution: For each element, look up its complement in the map; if found return both indices, otherwise record the current value and index.

problems.name: Contains Duplicate
problems.description: Return true if any value appears at least twice in the array.
hints: What structure makes membership checks cheap?
When should you return true immediately?
problems.approach: Insert elements into a hash set, returning true on the first insertion failure.
problems.solution: Scan and add each value to a set; if an element is already present, a duplicate exists and the answer is true.

problems.name: Intersection of Two Arrays
problems.description: Given two arrays, return their distinct common elements.
hints: Which array should you turn into a set?
How do you ensure the result has no duplicates?
problems.approach: Put one array in a set and collect elements of the other that are present.
problems.solution: Convert the smaller array to a set, iterate the other, and add to a result set every element found in it.

problems.name: Group Anagrams
problems.description: Given a list of strings, group words that are anagrams of each other.
hints: What canonical key do all anagrams share?
How do you map each word to its key?
problems.approach: Use the sorted form or a character-count tuple as a hash key to bucket words together.
problems.solution: For each word, compute a key from its sorted characters (or a frequency tuple) and append the word to the bucket for that key.

name: Prefix-sum + hashing problems
overview: Combining prefix sums with hashing solves a family of hard-looking subarray problems in linear time. The key insight is that a subarray sum equals the difference of two prefix sums, so 'find a subarray with property X' becomes 'find two prefixes that differ in the right way'.
why: These problems are favorite hard/medium interview questions because the O(n^2) brute force is obvious but the linear solution requires insight. The prefix-hash combo is a signature skill that separates strong candidates.
when: Reach for prefix sums plus hashing when a problem asks for subarrays with a given sum, the longest subarray with sum k, or counts of subarrays whose sum has a divisibility property.

concepts.name: Prefix difference identity
concepts.description: sum(i..j) = pref[j] - pref[i-1], so subarray sums reduce to differences of prefixes.

concepts.name: Complement prefix
concepts.description: To find sum k ending at j, look for a previous prefix equal to pref[j] - k.

concepts.name: Earliest occurrence
concepts.description: Storing only the first index of each prefix gives the longest valid subarray.

concepts.name: Counting occurrences
concepts.description: Storing counts of each prefix yields the number of valid subarrays.

concepts.name: Modular transformations
concepts.description: For divisibility constraints, store prefixes reduced modulo the divisor.

patterns.name: Count subarrays summing to k
patterns.description: Track prefix counts and look up the complement.

patterns.name: Longest subarray summing to k
patterns.description: Keep the earliest index where each prefix first appeared.

patterns.name: Count subarrays divisible by k
patterns.description: Store prefix counts by remainder mod k.

examples.title: Counting subarrays that sum to k
examples.problem: Count contiguous subarrays whose elements sum exactly to k.
examples.explanation: Prefixes are 1, 3, 6. Subarray [1,2] (prefixes 3-1=2 difference 2... tracing: pref 1 then pref 3 with pref-k=0 exists once) and subarray [3] (pref 6 with pref-k=3 exists) sum to 3, giving 2.
steps: Initialize running prefix and a map with {0: 1}.
For each element, add it to the running prefix.
Add the count of previous prefixes equal to prefix - k.
Record the current prefix count and continue.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to seed the map with {0: 1} for zero-length subarrays.
mistakes.fix: The empty prefix equals 0, so a whole-array or full-prefix match counts correctly only when 0 is pre-seeded.

mistakes.mistake: Storing prefix values after the lookup instead of before, missing the current subarray.
mistakes.fix: Look up the complement before recording the current prefix so subarrays ending here are counted.

mistakes.mistake: Using indices where counts are needed, or counts where earliest indices are needed.
mistakes.fix: Use counts when the number of subarrays is asked and earliest indices when the longest length is asked.

problems.name: Subarray Sum Equals K
problems.description: Count the number of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals k.
hints: How is a subarray sum expressed as two prefix sums?
What should you count in the hash map?
problems.approach: Maintain running prefix sums and a hash map of prefix counts, adding the count of prefix - k at each step.
problems.solution: Each prefix minus a previous prefix is a subarray sum. At each step add how many previous prefixes equal current - k, then record the current prefix.

problems.name: Maximum Size Subarray Sum Equals k
problems.description: Find the length of the longest subarray whose sum equals k.
hints: Which prefix value gives the longest match at index i?
Why store only the first occurrence of each prefix?
problems.approach: Store the earliest index of each prefix sum and compute the longest span to an earlier prefix equal to current - k.
problems.solution: Record only the first time each prefix appears. At each index, if prefix - k was seen, the length is i minus its first index; keep the max.

problems.name: Subarray Sums Divisible by K
problems.description: Count subarrays whose sum is divisible by k.
hints: What remainder property must two prefixes share?
How do you normalize negative remainders in Python?
problems.approach: Count prefix sums by their remainder modulo k; equal remainders mark divisible subarrays.
problems.solution: Two prefixes with the same remainder mod k differ by a multiple of k. Normalize remainders with % k (Python handles negatives) and sum the pair counts.

problems.name: Binary Subarrays With Sum
problems.description: Count binary subarrays whose sum equals a given goal.
hints: How does prefix counting apply to binary values?
Can you reuse the subarray-sum-equals-k idea?
problems.approach: Apply the prefix-sum plus hashing pattern directly, treating goal as k over a binary array.
problems.solution: Track running prefix counts and add the number of previous prefixes equal to prefix - goal at each step.

name: HashMap / HashSet
overview: HashMap and HashSet are the two concrete hash-based collections: a map stores key-value pairs while a set stores unique keys alone. They both provide average O(1) operations and are the go-to tools for membership, deduplication, and lookup problems.
why: Knowing when to pick a map versus a set is a frequent interview distinction, and both appear in an enormous share of easy and medium problems. Correctly choosing between them often determines whether a solution stays linear.
when: Reach for a HashSet when you only need to know if something exists. Reach for a HashMap when each key must be associated with data such as indices, counts, or values.

concepts.name: HashMap
concepts.description: A dictionary mapping unique keys to values with average O(1) access.

concepts.name: HashSet
concepts.description: A set of unique keys used for fast membership and deduplication.

concepts.name: Key requirements
concepts.description: Keys must be hashable and immutable, such as ints, strings, and tuples.

concepts.name: Overwrite semantics
concepts.description: Inserting an existing key in a map replaces its value; sets simply ignore the duplicate.

patterns.name: Index lookup map
patterns.description: Map values to their positions for O(1) index retrieval.

patterns.name: Membership set
patterns.description: Quickly test whether a value has appeared.
patterns.code:
def has_appeared(a, x):
    return x in set(a)

patterns.name: Value counting map
patterns.description: Count occurrences with get default.

examples.title: Building an index map
examples.problem: Store the position of each value in an array for fast lookups.
examples.explanation: Scanning left to right records each value's index, with later occurrences overwriting earlier ones for 'a'.
steps: Create an empty dictionary.
Iterate with both value and index.
Assign the index as the value for each key.
Return the completed map.

mistakes.mistake: Using a set when you need per-key data such as indices or counts.
mistakes.fix: Upgrade to a map (dict) whenever each key must carry associated information.

mistakes.mistake: Using a map when only membership matters, wasting memory and clarity.
mistakes.fix: Downshift to a set when the values would never be read.

mistakes.mistake: Trying to use mutable keys like lists in a dict or set.
mistakes.fix: Convert to an immutable form like a tuple before using it as a key.

problems.name: Contains Duplicate
problems.description: Return true if any value appears more than once.
hints: Which collection detects a repeat in O(1)?
Do you need any data besides membership?
problems.approach: Insert each element into a HashSet and return true on the first duplicate.
problems.solution: Add each value to a set; if an element is already present, a duplicate exists.

problems.name: Two Sum
problems.description: Find two numbers that sum to a target and return their indices.
hints: Why do you need a map rather than a set here?
What data rides along with each key?
problems.approach: Use a HashMap storing value-to-index and check for complements while scanning.
problems.solution: For each element, check if its complement exists in the map; if so return both indices, otherwise record the value with its index.

problems.name: Valid Sudoku
problems.description: Determine whether a 9x9 Sudoku board is valid without checking solvability.
hints: What three sets of constraints must be checked?
How do you key each 3x3 box?
problems.approach: Use HashSets for each row, column, and 3x3 box, rejecting duplicate digits.
problems.solution: Track seen digits per row, per column, and per box keyed by (r // 3, c // 3); any duplicate digit in a track makes the board invalid.

problems.name: Word Pattern
problems.description: Check whether a string follows a bijective mapping from pattern letters to words.
hints: What two mappings must be bijective?
Why check both directions?
problems.approach: Maintain a HashMap from pattern char to word and another from word to char, rejecting violations of injectivity.
problems.solution: Split the string into words; if pattern and words differ in length return false. Map each char to a word and each word to a char, failing on any conflict.

name: Frequency maps
overview: A frequency map (or Counter) maps each distinct element to the number of times it appears. It is the natural structure for 'how many times does X occur' questions and enables O(n) solutions to anagram, majority, and top-k problems.
why: Frequency maps are so common that interviewers routinely expect the Counter-based approach for anagrams, duplicates, and occurrence-counting problems. Demonstrating mastery of counting is a quick credibility win.
