when: Reach for a frequency map whenever you must answer questions about occurrence counts, most/least frequent values, or compare multisets of elements.

concepts.name: Build and query
concepts.description: One pass to increment counts, then O(1) queries per element.

concepts.name: Counter equality
concepts.description: Two collections match as multisets when their frequency maps are equal.

concepts.name: Decrement as consumption
concepts.description: Subtracting counts models using up occurrences, failing when counts go negative.

concepts.name: Top k selection
concepts.description: Sorting counts or using a heap extracts the most frequent elements.

patterns.name: Count and select max
patterns.description: Build counts, then find the highest count.

patterns.name: Build with defaultdict
patterns.description: Avoid get() boilerplate with a default factory.

patterns.name: Reconciling two strings
patterns.description: Increment for one string, decrement for the other.

examples.title: Finding the mode with a Counter
examples.problem: Return the most frequent element in an array.
examples.explanation: The Counter gives 3 a count of three, 1 a count of two, and 2 a count of one, so 3 is the mode.
steps: Build a Counter over the array.
Inspect the counts: 3 appears three times.
Select the entry with the largest count.
Return its key, which is 3.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to import Counter or misusing it on a non-iterable.
mistakes.fix: Counter expects an iterable; pass the collection itself, not a nested structure.

mistakes.mistake: Checking counts with m[ch] on a missing key, which inserts it or raises.
mistakes.fix: Use m.get(ch, 0) for lookups that should not mutate the map.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming frequency maps are sorted by count by default.
mistakes.fix: Use most_common() or sort by value; plain iteration order is insertion order.

problems.name: Ransom Note
problems.description: Check whether a magazine contains enough letters to build a ransom note.
hints: Which letters and how many does the note need?
When does the magazine run out?
problems.approach: Count magazine letters, then consume them per note letter and fail on a shortfall.
problems.solution: Build a Counter from the magazine, decrement per note character, and return false whenever a count would go negative.

problems.name: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
problems.description: Design a class that returns the k-th largest element from a stream of numbers added over time.
hints: Which heap size keeps the k-th largest at the top?
When should an added value be ignored?
problems.approach: Maintain a min-heap of size k so the smallest element in the heap is the k-th largest overall.
problems.solution: Push each value into a min-heap; when the heap exceeds k, pop the smallest. The heap top is always the k-th largest.

problems.name: Sort Characters By Frequency
problems.description: Sort a string by character frequency in decreasing order.
hints: What do you build first to know each count?
How do you rebuild the string in frequency order?
problems.approach: Count characters, sort by count descending, and repeat each character that many times.
problems.solution: Build a Counter, sort its items by frequency, and join each character repeated its count times.

problems.name: Find All Duplicates in an Array
problems.description: Given an array where values are in range [1, n], return all values appearing twice.
hints: How does the value range help with indexing?
Can a frequency map do this in O(n)?
problems.approach: Count frequencies and collect elements whose count equals two.
problems.solution: Build a Counter over the array and return every key whose count is exactly two; the value range guarantees such keys always exist.

name: Collision concepts
overview: A collision occurs when two distinct keys hash to the same table slot, and how a hash table resolves collisions determines its worst-case behavior. The two classic strategies are chaining, where each slot holds a linked list or other structure, and open addressing, which probes to find alternate slots.
why: Understanding collisions explains why hash operations are O(1) on average but can degrade to O(n), and why Python's dict and set stay fast in practice. Interviewers occasionally probe this to test whether you know more than the API.
when: Reach for collision concepts when designing a custom hash table, analyzing worst-case inputs, or comparing hashing strategies. Know that good load factors and hash functions keep average cases near O(1).

complexity.time: O(1) average, O(n) worst case per operation

concepts.name: Collision
concepts.description: Two distinct keys landing on the same bucket after hashing.

concepts.name: Chaining
concepts.description: Each bucket stores a linked structure of keys that hash to it; lookup scans that chain.

concepts.name: Open addressing
concepts.description: The table itself stores one value per slot; collisions probe linearly or quadratically for the next free slot.

concepts.name: Load factor
concepts.description: The fraction of occupied slots; higher load factors raise collision probability and slow lookups.

concepts.name: Resizing
concepts.description: Growing the table when the load factor exceeds a threshold to restore average O(1) operations.

concepts.name: Hash function quality
concepts.description: A good hash function spreads keys evenly; a weak one clusters them and degrades performance.

patterns.name: Chained hash table
patterns.description: A list of buckets, each a list of (key, value) pairs.

patterns.name: Linear probing
patterns.description: Find the next free slot by walking forward and wrapping around.

examples.title: Chaining resolves a collision
examples.problem: Insert keys that hash to the same bucket and explain how lookups still work.
examples.input: buckets = 2, keys = 10 and 12 hashing to bucket 0
examples.explanation: Both keys hash to bucket 0, so they are stored as a two-element chain. A lookup for 12 must scan the chain to distinguish it from 10.
steps: Hash each key to a bucket index.
Append the colliding key to the bucket's chain.
On lookup, compare each chain element by key equality.
The chain length equals the number of colliding keys.

mistakes.mistake: Claiming hash operations are always O(1) with no caveats.
mistakes.fix: Say average O(1) and note the O(n) worst case when many keys collide.

mistakes.mistake: Treating the hash value as the final index without taking a modulus.
mistakes.fix: Reduce the hash to the table size with hash % size so it lands within bounds.

mistakes.mistake: Using a weak hash function that clusters similar keys together.
mistakes.fix: Design the hash to spread keys evenly, or rely on a language-standard hash such as Python's.

problems.name: Design HashMap
problems.description: Design a hash map supporting put, get, and remove with a fixed-size array of buckets.
problems.constraints: 1 <= operations <= 10^4, keys in a bounded integer range
hints: How do you map a key to a bucket index?
What structure resolves keys that share a bucket?
problems.approach: Use chaining with an array of buckets; map each key to a bucket by modulus and manage the chain.
problems.solution: Buckets hold lists of key-value pairs. Put updates or appends, get scans the bucket for the key, and remove deletes the matching pair.

problems.name: Design HashSet
problems.description: Design a hash set supporting add, contains, and remove.
hints: How is a set like a map without values?
What handles keys that land in the same bucket?
problems.approach: Chain keys in buckets, adding only if absent and removing by equality.
problems.solution: Store keys as a list of buckets; contains checks membership, add inserts if missing, remove deletes the matching key.

problems.name: Analyze worst-case hashing
problems.description: Given a bad hash function that maps everything to one bucket, analyze lookup complexity.
hints: How long does a chain get when everything collides?
What does that imply for a single lookup?
problems.approach: All keys land in one chain, so a lookup may scan all of them.
problems.solution: With every key in a single bucket, the chain holds n entries and a lookup can degrade to scanning all of them, hence O(n) worst case.

name: Hashing with arrays/strings
overview: Hashing is the standard companion to array and string problems, enabling membership checks, frequency counts, and complement lookups that turn quadratic scans into linear ones. The data being hashed is usually array elements, characters, or substrings.
why: The majority of array and string interview problems are solved with a hash map or set in the loop, so knowing how to hash integers, characters, and longer keys is a core skill. It directly unlocks two-sum, anagrams, and duplicate detection.
when: Reach for hashing when an array or string problem needs repeated lookups, counts of characters or values, or pair/complement detection that a naive double loop would handle slowly.

concepts.name: Hashing array values
concepts.description: Storing numbers or objects from an array for O(1) membership and lookup.

concepts.name: Hashing characters
concepts.description: Using characters as keys for frequency and comparison problems.

concepts.name: String keys
concepts.description: Hashing whole strings or their sorted/frequency forms to group related words.

concepts.name: Complement lookup
concepts.description: Storing seen values so the partner needed to complete a condition is found in O(1).

patterns.name: Character frequency
patterns.description: Count character occurrences for anagram and uniqueness checks.

patterns.name: Seen-set deduplication
patterns.description: Skip elements already seen while scanning a list.

patterns.name: Complement with arrays
patterns.description: Look up the needed partner for each element.

examples.title: Hashing characters for uniqueness
examples.problem: Return true if a string contains all distinct characters.
examples.explanation: Hashing each character into a set detects the duplicate 'a', so the string is not all-distinct.
steps: Initialize an empty set.
Visit each character of the string.
If already in the set, return false.
Otherwise add it and continue, returning true at the end.

mistakes.mistake: Using a set when the index or count of each element is also needed.
mistakes.fix: Upgrade to a dictionary mapping the key to its index or count.

mistakes.mistake: Building a hash structure repeatedly inside a loop instead of once.
mistakes.fix: Precompute the map or set before the main loop and only query it inside.

mistakes.mistake: Using mutable strings or lists as hash keys.
mistakes.fix: Keys must be immutable; use tuples or normalized strings for compound keys.

problems.name: First Unique Character in a String
problems.description: Return the index of the first non-repeating character in a string, or -1 if none exists.
hints: What must you know before you can detect uniqueness?
How many passes over the string do you need?
problems.approach: Count characters with a hash map in one pass, then rescan for the first character with count 1.
problems.solution: Build a frequency map, then walk the string again returning the index of the first character whose count equals 1.

problems.name: Two Sum
problems.description: Return the indices of two numbers that add to a target.
hints: Which seen values should you remember and how?
What complement finishes the pair?
problems.approach: Store each value's index in a hash map and check for the target minus the current value.
problems.solution: For each element, look up its complement; if present return both indices, otherwise store the value with its index.

problems.name: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.description: Find the length of the longest substring with all distinct characters.
hints: How do you remember the last position of each character?
Where does the window restart on a repeat?
problems.approach: Keep a map of the last seen index per character and slide a window, jumping its left edge past repeats.
problems.solution: Scan with a window; when a character repeats inside the window, move the left edge just past its prior occurrence using the stored index map.

problems.name: Group Anagrams
problems.description: Group words that are anagrams of one another.
hints: What key represents a group of anagrams?
How do you compute that key from a word?
problems.approach: Key each word by its sorted characters and bucket words under matching keys.
problems.solution: Sort each word's letters to form a canonical key (or build a frequency tuple) and append the word to that key's bucket.
